transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Fitzgerald, thank you for agreeing to speak with me. I've asked your nurse to step out for a few minutes so we have some privacy.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, is everything alright? I'm just... I'm feeling a bit tired.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to be very honest with you about something that happened during your surgery. We made a mistake. We skipped a step in verifying your blood type before your transfusion, and as a result, you received a blood type that was compatible, but not the ideal match for your specific type.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I... what? You gave me the wrong blood?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am so sorry. This was our error, and we failed to follow the safety checks that are in place to prevent this from happening. I take full responsibility for this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My goodness. I can't... I just can't believe this. My husband, Arthur, he always used to say I was the clumsy one, but I'm the one lying here and you're the doctors. How could this happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely understandable that you feel shocked. It is a heavy thing to hear, especially when you trusted us with your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: He would have known what to do. Arthur always handled the paperwork, the appointments. I feel so small without him here to tell me if this is something I should be terrified of.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like Arthur was your rock in these situations, and not having him by your side right now makes this feel even more overwhelming.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It does. It really does. I just... I'm shaking. Is the wrong blood going to kill me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: To answer your question clearly, because it is a scary thought: no, the blood you received was compatible, meaning it won't cause a severe rejection reaction. However, it wasn't the perfect match we should have given you. Does that make sense, or can I explain that part differently?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Compatible... so it doesn't fight me? But it's still not right.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Exactly. It is safe in your system, but it's not what the protocol requires. I want to make sure I've been clear—do you feel you understand why we're having this conversation, or is there any part of the blood type issue that feels confusing?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I think I get it. You missed a check. You gave me the second-best option. I just feel so let down. I've been so careful with everything since he passed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear how disappointing and frightening this is. You've been doing everything right, and we failed to do our part. There is no excuse for skipping that verification step.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What are you going to do now? Am I going to get sick?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are monitoring your vitals and your blood work very closely. Right now, you are stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what? Who is checking? How do I know it won't happen again tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We're looking into it. We'll be doing some more tests and we'll see what the investigation says.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When? Who is doing the tests?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The team is on it. We will probably have some news soon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Soon isn't a time. Do I need to call anyone? Do I need to write something down?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I think we just need to wait and see how your body reacts. We'll keep an eye on you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want to just wait. I want to know there's a plan. Arthur would have had a list. He always had a list of questions.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you want a concrete plan. We'll just keep monitoring you for now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But what happens if something goes wrong tonight?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The nurses are watching you. We'll just stay tuned to the lab results.

H.justification: The resident allows the patient to finish all turns, maintains a regulated pace during distress, and never interrupts.

E.justification: The error is named in the second turn, lay language is used, and comprehension is checked twice ('Does that make sense', 'do you feel you understand').

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language ('I am so sorry'), takes full responsibility, and maintains this accountability throughout the pushback.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('shocked', 'disappointing and frightening') and engages with the patient's shared content regarding her husband Arthur.

T.justification: The resident provides only placeholders and vague responses ('looking into it', 'news soon', 'stay tuned') without timelines, patient roles, or prevention details.
